prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Cyclist Lance Armstrong said Thursday the surgery to repair his broken collarbone proved to be more complex than doctors originally anticipated and that he will take his recovery "day by day." Cyclist Lance Armstrong needed 12 screws to repair his broken collarbone. "I thought everything went very smooth," he said in a video to his supporters about Wednesday's three-hour operation. Doctors in Spain, where Armstrong injured himself Monday when he fell during a race, initially thought he had suffered a simple fracture. However, additional X-rays and CT scans in Austin, Texas, where he lives, proved otherwise. "They realized that the collarbone is actually in quite a few pieces," said the 37-year-old cyclist, who pointed to an X-ray of a 4- to 5-inch steel plate held in place by a dozen 1-inch screws, intended to stabilize it. "That should keep things together," he said. "Ultimately, that will have to come out, but for now, it's necessary."  Watch how Armstrong "tweets" from hospital » . Armstrong said he felt "very lucky, very blessed" that, in almost 20 years of professional cycling, he has rarely crashed. "We don't know how my recovery will go, we'll just take it day by day and ultimately get back on the bike and try to sort things out." Armstrong's remarks came a day after his surgeon, Dr. Douglas Elenz, told reporters that the cyclist will require two to three months of healing. The four breaks "made treatment more challenging, but we're confident that the treatment performed today is going to be successful," Elenz said. During the next week, Armstrong "will need to take it easy" to ensure the wound does not become infected, the doctor said. After his wound has healed, Armstrong will begin using an exercise bike to train his lower body, "but we won't let him do a whole lot with his upper extremities," Elenz said. "After several weeks, we can take his training to the street, but we will need to take that day by day and week by week." He said that, over the longer term, he will be looking for evidence that Armstrong is laying down new bone, that the plate is stable, that the athlete's arm is strong and that his motion is fluid. Armstrong, riding for Team Astana, crashed about 10 miles (16 kilometers) from the end of the first stage of the five-day Vuelta Ciclista a Castilla y Leon race.  Watch Armstrong's crash » . Armstrong announced last year that he was returning to competitive biking and would use the Spanish race as a warm-up for the Tour de France, which he won seven times before retiring in 2005. He also had planned to race May 9-31 in the Giro d'Italia, one of Europe's most prestigious and grueling stage races. This would have been the second comeback of his career. His first came in 1998, two years after he was diagnosed with advanced testicular cancer that had spread to his lungs and brain. Doctors gave him a less than 50 percent chance of survival.

(CNN) — Lance Armstrong said Thursday that repairing his fractured collarbone was more complicated than physicians had first expected. He added that he would evaluate his recovery one day at a time.

The cyclist’s collarbone required a steel plate and 12 screws. Speaking to supporters in a video after Wednesday’s three-hour surgery, Armstrong said he believed the procedure had gone very well.

Doctors in Spain initially diagnosed the injury as a straightforward fracture. Armstrong was hurt there Monday after falling during a race. But further X-rays and CT scans in Austin, Texas, where he lives, revealed that the bone had broken into several pieces.

“They realized that the collarbone is actually in quite a few pieces,” the 37-year-old said while indicating an X-ray. It showed a steel plate measuring roughly 4 to 5 inches, secured by twelve 1-inch screws to hold the bone in place.

“That should keep things together,” Armstrong said. He explained that the hardware would eventually need to be removed but was necessary for the time being.

A related video showed Armstrong posting updates on Twitter from the hospital.

Armstrong said he felt “very lucky, very blessed” because he had experienced few crashes during nearly two decades as a professional cyclist.

“We don’t know how my recovery will go,” he said, adding that he would proceed day by day before returning to his bicycle and figuring out the next steps.

His comments came one day after his surgeon, Dr. Douglas Elenz, told journalists that healing would take between two and three months. Elenz said the collarbone’s four separate breaks complicated the treatment, but he was confident that the operation would succeed.

According to the doctor, Armstrong would have to rest during the following week to reduce the risk of infection at the surgical site. Once the wound healed, he could begin training his lower body on a stationary bicycle, though he would be prevented from doing much with his upper limbs.

Elenz said Armstrong might be able to resume outdoor training after several weeks, but his progress would have to be assessed both day by day and week by week. Over time, the surgeon would monitor whether new bone was forming, the plate remained secure, Armstrong’s arm regained strength, and his movement became smooth.

Armstrong, competing for Team Astana, crashed approximately 10 miles, or 16 kilometers, before the finish of the opening stage of the five-day Vuelta Ciclista a Castilla y Leon. Another video showed the crash.

The previous year, Armstrong had announced his return to competitive cycling. He intended to use the event in Spain as preparation for the Tour de France, a race he had won seven times before retiring in 2005.

He had also planned to compete in the Giro d’Italia from May 9 through May 31. The event is regarded as one of Europe’s most prestigious and demanding multistage races.

This marked what would have been Armstrong’s second career comeback. His first occurred in 1998, two years after he was diagnosed with advanced testicular cancer that had spread to both his lungs and his brain. At the time, doctors estimated that his likelihood of surviving was below 50 percent.

**Armstrong’s fractured collarbone puts Giro start in doubt, but Tour remains realistic**

**AUSTIN, Texas — March 26, 2009** — Lance Armstrong’s comeback has encountered its first major obstacle after the seven-time Tour de France champion underwent surgery to repair a fractured right collarbone suffered in a crash at Spain’s Vuelta a Castilla y León.

Armstrong, 37, was injured Monday when several riders went down during the opening stage near Baltanás. He landed heavily on his right shoulder and was taken to a hospital in Valladolid, where X-rays confirmed a fracture of the clavicle. He then returned to the United States for surgery in Austin.

“I guess this is what you call a setback,” Armstrong wrote after the crash, while also reassuring followers with the brief message: “I’m alive!”

The operation revealed a more complicated injury than initial examinations had suggested. Orthopedic surgeon Dr. Doug Elenz said Armstrong’s collarbone was broken into multiple pieces and required a metal plate and screws to stabilize it.

“It was a bit more challenging than we thought,” Elenz said. “It was broken in four pieces.”

Elenz said the procedure went well but cautioned that Armstrong’s return would depend on bone healing, pain control and his ability to regain strength and movement in the shoulder. Although elite cyclists can often resume stationary-bike training relatively quickly after a collarbone fracture, outdoor riding presents greater risks. Another fall before the bone has healed could dislodge the repair or cause a new fracture near the plate.

### Giro timetable is tight

The injury immediately placed Armstrong’s planned debut in the Giro d’Italia in jeopardy. The Italian race was scheduled to begin May 9, leaving less than seven weeks between surgery and the opening stage.

That timetable is aggressive for a complicated clavicle fracture. Armstrong could maintain much of his cardiovascular fitness on an indoor trainer, but road racing requires more than aerobic conditioning. He must be able to pull on the handlebars while climbing, absorb shocks from rough pavement, steer confidently in a crowded peloton and protect himself in the event of another crash.

Armstrong nevertheless indicated that he did not want to abandon the Giro without first seeing how quickly he recovered.

“The Giro is still very much a possibility,” he said, while acknowledging that the injury would force him to adjust his training.

Even if Armstrong makes the start, his competitive goals may have to change. Before the crash, the Giro was expected to be both a major target and an important test of his form following more than three years away from professional cycling. With training interrupted, he could instead use the race to rebuild endurance and support Astana teammate Levi Leipheimer rather than pursue the overall title.

The Giro’s three-week length could also work in Armstrong’s favor if he is medically cleared to start. Riders often improve as a grand tour progresses, and Armstrong would have additional time to recover before the decisive mountain stages. But the opening days would carry obvious danger: a crash in the tightly packed field could damage the healing shoulder and threaten the rest of his season.

### Tour de France outlook more encouraging

The Tour de France, beginning July 4, appeared to be under much less threat. Armstrong had more than three months to recover, providing a significantly larger margin for the fracture to unite and for him to restore upper-body strength.

“I don’t think the Tour is in jeopardy at all,” Armstrong said.

Elenz offered a similarly cautious but optimistic assessment. The surgeon said Armstrong should be able to resume some training quickly, though full healing would take longer. A typical recovery window for this type of injury is roughly eight to 12 weeks, depending on X-rays, symptoms and the demands placed on the shoulder.

For Armstrong, the central issue may be less whether he can ride the Tour than whether he can arrive in France with enough racing in his legs to contend. His comeback had been designed around a steady progression of stage races leading into the Giro and then the Tour. The crash disrupts that schedule at a critical point, potentially costing him both training intensity and competitive sharpness.

It also complicates Astana’s leadership picture. Alberto Contador, the 2007 Tour winner, was already expected to be the team’s principal contender in France. Armstrong’s injury could make it harder for him to establish himself as a co-leader, particularly if he reaches July without completing the Giro or another demanding stage race.

Still, Armstrong has built his career around meticulous preparation and rapid rehabilitation. The plate stabilizing the collarbone may allow him to begin controlled indoor work within days, provided pain and swelling subside. From there, his medical team will monitor the incision, shoulder mobility and evidence of bone healing before allowing him back onto the road.

The immediate objective is straightforward: protect the repair and preserve as much fitness as possible. The Giro remains a race against the calendar. The Tour, barring complications, remains a realistic target.

Armstrong’s comeback has not been stopped, but after the crash in Spain, it has become considerably more difficult.
